'''Wang Xiji''' ({{zh|c=王希季|w=Wang Hsi-chi}}; 26 July 1921 – 12 August 2026) was a Chinese aerospace engineer. The chief designer of China's first [[sounding rocket]] ([[T-7 (rocket)|T-7]]), first [[space launch vehicle]] ([[Long March 1]]) and first recoverable satellites,<ref name="Stokes" /> he was awarded the [[Two Bombs, One Satellite]] Meritorious Medal in 1999. He was an academician of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] and the [[International Academy of Astronautics]],<ref name=":2" /> and was inducted into the [[International Astronautical Federation]] Hall of Fame in 2016.<ref name=":5" />

== Early life and education ==
Wang was born on 26 July 1921 into a merchant family in [[Kunming]], Yunnan, China.<ref name="u342">{{cite web | title=Muere Wang Xiji a los 105 años, pionero del programa espacial de China | publisher=Descubriendo China | date=14 August 2026 | url=https://www.descubriendochina.org/post/muere-wang-xiji-pionero-programa-espacial-chino | language=es | access-date=15 August 2026}}</ref><ref name="i375">{{cite web | last=Lei | first=Zhao | title=Space industry pioneer Wang Xiji dies at 105 | publisher=China Daily | date=14 August 2026 | url=https://global.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202608/14/WS6a7e7126a31073853ec53413.html | access-date=15 August 2026}}</ref> He was a member of the [[Bai people|Bai ethnic minority]] from [[Dali Bai Autonomous Prefecture]].<ref name="Stokes">{{Cite book|url=https://ssi.armywarcollege.edu/pdffiles/PUB52.pdf|title=The Lessons of History: The Chinese people's Liberation Army at 75|last=Stokes|first=Mark A.|date=July 2003|publisher=[[Strategic Studies Institute]]|isbn=978-1-58487-126-2|editor1=Laurie Burkitt|pages=235|chapter=The People's Liberation Army and China's Space and Missile Development|editor2=Andrew Scobell|editor3=[[Larry Wortzel]]|archive-date=8 February 2012|access-date=29 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120208090353/http://www.strategicstudiesinstitute.army.mil/pdffiles/PUB52.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.spacechina.com/n25/n2014703/n2014718/n2014752/c2017719/content.html|title=王希季院士|date=31 October 2011|website=China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation|access-date=29 May 2019|archive-date=29 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190529090220/http://www.spacechina.com/n25/n2014703/n2014718/n2014752/c2017719/content.html|url-status=live}}</ref> He graduated from the Department of Mechanical Engineering of [[National Southwestern Associated University]] in 1942,<ref name=":0" /> and went to the United States in 1948 to study at the [[Virginia Polytechnic Institute]],<ref name="Stokes" /> earning his master's degree in 1949. When the [[People's Republic of China]] was founded, he abandoned his doctoral studies and returned to China in 1950.<ref name="Stokes" /><ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
=== Sounding rockets ===
{{Main|T-7 (rocket)}}
[[File:Zhongguo Diyimei Zixing Sheji Zhizaode Shiyan Tankong Huojian T-7M Fashechang Yizhi.jpg|thumb|Monument for the T-7M, China's first sounding rocket, in Laogang, [[Pudong]], Shanghai]]

After returning to China, Wang taught at the [[Dalian Institute of Technology]], [[Shanghai Jiao Tong University]], and [[Shanghai University of Science and Technology]].<ref name=":0" /> In 1958, when Wang was serving as professor and vice chair of the Department of Engineering Mechanics at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, he was abruptly appointed chief engineer of the [[Shanghai Institute of Mechanical and Electrical Engineering]]. Only after he arrived at his new workplace did he learn that China had started its satellite program and the institute was responsible for developing rockets for satellite launches.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.cas.cn/zt/sszt/yq60/ldyx/jzhdz/wxj/|title=箭击长空忆当年|last=Wang|first=Xiji|date=August 1999|website=Chinese Academy of Sciences|access-date=29 May 2019|archive-date=29 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211229105238/https://www.cas.cn/zt/sszt/yq60/ldyx/jzhdz/wxj/|url-status=live}}</ref> The institute had very few experienced scientists. Other than Wang Xiji and his former classmate {{ill|Yang Nansheng|zh|杨南生}}, who was the deputy director of the institute, there were only two visiting professors, [[Bian Yingui]] (卞荫贵) and [[Li Minhua]].<ref name=":1" /> The rest of the institute consisted of a few hundred university students with an average age of 21. Even Wang and Yang had little knowledge about rockets and had to learn on the fly.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://www.china.com.cn/chinese/TEC-c/42406.htm|title="两弹一星"功勋奖章获得者航天技术专家王希季|date=4 April 2001|website=People's Daily Overseas Edition|access-date=30 May 2019|archive-date=17 July 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070717140226/http://www.china.com.cn/chinese/TEC-c/42406.htm|url-status=live}}</ref>

Working with severe shortages of technical experience, funds, and equipment, Wang's team managed to develop China's first [[sounding rocket]], the [[T-7 (rocket)|T-7M]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> After a failed first launch in January 1960, the second launch on 19 February 1960 was successful.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> Wang later developed 12 types of sounding rockets, including many recoverable and reusable designs.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://www.astronautix.com/w/wangxiji.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161228151322/http://astronautix.com/w/wangxiji.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=28 December 2016|title=Wang Xiji|website=Astronautix.com|access-date=30 May 2019}}</ref>

=== Space launch vehicle and recoverable satellites ===
In the 1960s, Wang proposed the design for the [[Long March 1]], China's first [[space launch vehicle]], which launched China's first satellite, the [[Dong Fang Hong I]], in 1970.<ref name=":2" /> He subsequently led the design of China's first recoverable satellite, the [[Jian Bing 1]].<ref name=":2" /> After an initial failure in 1974, it was successfully launched in 1975, making China the third country in the world to launch a recoverable satellite.<ref name=":3" /> Wang's recoverable satellites achieved a higher success rate than the [[Corona (satellite)|Corona (Discoverer)]] program of the United States and the [[Zenit (satellite)|Zenit series]] of the Soviet Union.<ref name=":3" />

=== Crewed spacecraft ===
In the late 1960s, Wang proposed the [[Shuguang (spacecraft)|Shuguang]] project for [[crewed spacecraft]]. Although initially approved by [[Mao Zedong]], it was later cancelled in 1973 due to a shortage of funds. When China restarted the [[Shenzhou program]] in 1992, Wang served as a senior supervisor of the project, which succeeded in putting [[Yang Liwei|the first Chinese astronaut]] into orbit in 2003.<ref name=":2" />

=== Other programs ===
In 2002, Wang chaired a national policy committee that created a report outlining the future directions for the space and missile programs of China.<ref name="Stokes" />

In 2015, Wang proposed building a [[space-based solar power]] station with at least {{convert|5|-|6|km2}} of [[solar panels]], {{Convert|36000|km||abbr=}} above earth.<ref name=":4" /> The energy would be transmitted to earth in the form of [[microwave]] or [[laser]]. The idea first appeared in [[Isaac Asimov]]'s 1941 [[science fiction]] short story "[[Reason (short story)|Reason]]".<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=http://english.cas.cn/newsroom/news/201503/t20150331_145878.shtml|title=Chinese Scientists Mull Power Station in Space|last=Chen|first=Na|date=31 March 2015|website=Chinese Academy of Sciences|access-date=30 May 2019|archive-date=30 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190530224121/http://english.cas.cn/newsroom/news/201503/t20150331_145878.shtml|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Wang was married to Nie Xiufang, with whom he had two daughters.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sohu.com/a/1063556001_122481575?scm=10001.325_13-325_13.0.0-0-0-0-0.5_1334&spm=smpc.channel_248.block3_308_NDdFbm_1_fd.4.1786838400012DA5oXoZ_324&_trans_=000014_bdss_dkgyxqsP3p:CP=Google%20search%20indexing |title='两弹一星'元勋王希季逝世，享年105岁！他与结发妻子恩爱一生 |trans-title=Wang Xiji, a pioneer of China's 'Two Bombs, One Satellite' program, has passed away at the age of 105. He and his wife shared a lifetime of love and happiness.|newspaper=Sohu|date=16 August 2026|access-date=18 August 2026|lang=zh}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.tsinghua.org.cn/info/1023/31442.htm|title= 一个白族科学家的初心使命——记“两弹一星”元勋、中科院院士王希季 |trans-title=The Original Aspiration and Mission of a Bai Scientist – Remembering Wang Xiji, a Hero of the "Two Bombs, One Satellite" Project and Academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.|newspaper=Tsinghua Alumni Association|date=5 August 2019|access-date=18 August 2026|lang=zh}}</ref> Wang [[Centenarian|turned 100]] in July 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://min.news/en/military/7061b49e4ea429d84578cda2d492a9a0.html|title=The oldest "two bomb stars" father ushered in his 100th birthday}}</ref>

He died on 12 August 2026 in Beijing, at the age of 105.<ref>{{Cite web |title=国家"两弹一星功勋奖章"获得者王希季院士逝世，享年105岁 |url=https://m.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_33775307 |access-date=13 August 2026 |website=m.thepaper.cn |archive-date=13 August 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260813210101/https://m.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_33775307 |url-status=live }}</ref> His funeral was held on 20 August at [[Babaoshan Revolutionary Cemetery]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://finance.sina.com.cn/wm/2026-08-14/doc-ininhaiq4227482.shtml?froms=ggmp|title=“两弹一星功勋奖章”获得者王希季同志遗体告别仪式定于8月20日上午9时在北京八宝山殡仪馆大礼堂举行|trans-title=The memorial service for Comrade Wang Xiji, recipient of the "Two Bombs, One Satellite" Medal of Honor, will be held at 9:00 AM on August 20th in the Grand Hall of the Babaoshan Funeral Home in Beijing.|lang=zh|newspaper=Sina|date=14 August 2026|access-date=18 August 2026}}</ref>

== Honours and recognition ==
Wang was elected an academician of the [[International Academy of Astronautics]]<ref name=":4" /> and the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] in 1993.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.chinavitae.com/biography/Wang_Xiji/full|title=Biography of Wang Xiji|website=China Vitae|access-date=30 May 2019|archive-date=30 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190530193645/http://www.chinavitae.com/biography/Wang_Xiji/full|url-status=live}}</ref>

He was twice conferred the Special Prize of the [[State Science and Technology Progress Award]] (in 1985 and 1990),<ref name=":1" /> in addition to a First Class prize and a Second Class prize.<ref name=":2" /> He was awarded the [[Ho Leung Ho Lee Foundation|Ho Leung Ho Lee Prize]] for science and technology progress in 1995.<ref name="HLHL">{{cite web |title=何梁何利基金 {{!}} 王希季 |url=https://www.hlhl.org.cn/contents/2/36.html |website=www.hlhl.org.cn |publisher=[[Ho Leung Ho Lee Foundation]] |access-date=17 August 2026}}</ref> In 1999, Wang was awarded the [[Two Bombs, One Satellite]] Meritorious Medal.<ref name=":2" /> In 2016, he became the first Chinese inductee into the [[International Astronautical Federation]] Hall of Fame.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=http://www.iafastro.org/activities/honours-awards/hall-of-fame/|title=IAF Hall of Fame|publisher=International Astronautical Federation|access-date=30 October 2019|archive-date=6 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200306073527/http://www.iafastro.org/activities/honours-awards/hall-of-fame/|url-status=live}}</ref>
